title: Elementary Grammar (Essential Grammar in Use - Murphy)
lesson_overview: A2 level builds on A1 foundations, introducing past, future, and more complex structures for everyday communication.

topics.name: Past Simple
topics.lesson_text: Past Simple describes completed actions at a definite time in the past. Regular verbs: add -ed or -d. Irregular verbs: changes form completely (see list). Positive: I/you/he/she/it/we/they + past form. Negative: I/you/he/she/it/we/they + did not + base verb. Question: Did + I/you/he/she/it/we/they + base verb?. Time expressions: yesterday, last week, in 2010, ago., two ago.
examples: She bought a new car last month.

topics.name: Present Perfect
topics.lesson_text: Present Perfect connects past to present. Used for: life experience (I have ever been to...), recent actions (I have just done), ongoing situation (I have known him for...), with ever/never, already/just, for/since. Structure: have/has + past participle. Regular past participles: add -ed. Irregular: changes form. Note: Already = before the main verb or after 'not'. Just = immediately before the main verb.
examples: I have known him for years.

topics.name: Future Forms
topics.focus: will, going to, present continuous for future
topics.lesson_text: Future with will: spontaneous decisions, predictions, promises. Future with going to: intentions, plans based on evidence. Present continuous for future: arrangements already made. Structure: will + base verb. be + going to + base verb. be + -ing for future. Note: will not = won't. Going to not = not going to.
examples: I will help you with that.
We are flying to New York tomorrow.
key_concepts: will vs going to vs present continuous

topics.name: Modals (can/could/must)
topics.lesson_text: Can: ability, opportunity, request, permission. Could: past ability, polite suggestion, possibility. Must: strong obligation, necessity. Don't have to: not necessary. Must not: forbidden. Structure: modal + base verb (no 'to' after modal except have to). Negative: can't, couldn't, mustn't, don't have to. Note: Can't = cannot. Could have + past participle = missed possibility.
examples: You must stop at the red light.

cefr_description: Can communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a direct exchange of information.
